structured.recommendation: Adopt a progressive-delivery (canary) rollout with automated rollback tied to health SLOs. Canary rollout directly reduces deployment risk (issue:L1) by limiting blast radius to a small traffic percentage before full promotion, while preserving delivery speed (issue:L2) because promotion is automated on healthy signals rather than gated on manual approval. This answers the balance question (issue:L3) better than an all-or-nothing policy. However, the issue gives no baseline (current failure rate, deploy frequency, rollback cost), so I recommend committing to canary as the mechanism but treating specific thresholds (canary %, bake time, abort criteria) as provisional until those metrics are supplied.

evidence.claim: Primary goal is reducing deployment risk
Delivery speed must be preserved as a constraint
The open question is which policy balances risk and speed
Canary/progressive delivery limits blast radius and supports automated rollback, balancing risk and throughput

assumptions.statement: The deployment target can serve two versions concurrently and split traffic (or shift it incrementally).
assumptions.if_false_then: Canary is infeasible; fall back to blue/green or staged environment rollout, which trades some speed for isolation.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Check whether the runtime/platform supports weighted routing or multiple concurrent versions.

assumptions.statement: There are observable health/SLO signals fast enough to gate automated promotion and rollback.
assumptions.if_false_then: Automated canary abort cannot work; rollout risk reduction degrades to manual monitoring, hurting speed.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Confirm error-rate/latency metrics and alerting exist with low enough latency to catch regressions during bake time.

risks: Issue provides no baseline metrics, so any specific threshold (canary %, bake time) is unjustified and could be too aggressive or too slow.
Canary adds infrastructure and observability complexity; without mature monitoring it can create false confidence.
If rollback is not automated, canary preserves risk exposure while slowing delivery — the worst of both.
Stateful/schema-changing deploys break simple canary assumptions and need expand-contract migration, not addressed by the issue.
what_would_change_my_view: Baseline data showing current deploys already have very low failure rates, making canary overhead unjustified.
Platform constraints that prevent concurrent-version traffic splitting, favoring blue/green or ring-based rollout.
Evidence that changes are predominantly stateful/migration-heavy, shifting the answer toward migration strategy over traffic policy.
structured.next_action: Request the three missing baselines — current change-failure rate, deploy frequency, and mean rollback time — to set concrete canary percentage and bake-time thresholds.
